concept.name: Economic surprise index
concept.definition: An index that aggregates how economic data releases compare with consensus forecasts, turning 'better or worse than expected' into a single daily time series. The best known is the Citigroup Economic Surprise Index, a rolling three-month, weighted measure of data surprises versus Bloomberg survey medians.
concept.intuition: Markets move on surprises, not levels - the index tracks whether the flow of data is beating or disappointing what economists had already priced in.
concept.mechanics: Each release's surprise is the actual value minus the survey median, normalized by the historical standard deviation of surprises; the index sums these standardized surprises over a rolling three-month window, weighting indicators by their historical impact on high-frequency FX moves and applying a time decay so recent surprises count more.
concept.formula: ESI = Sum over releases of w_i x (Actual_i - Consensus_i) / sigma_i, computed daily over a trailing three-month window with FX-impact weights and time decay.
concept.failure_modes: It is mean-reverting by construction - a long run of beats pulls consensus up until misses become arithmetically likely - and it measures deviation from forecast, not whether the economy is actually strong or weak.
concept.misconceptions: A positive reading does not mean the economy is good, only better than expected; a deeply negative index can coincide with solid growth if consensus was simply too optimistic.
concept.example: The Citi U.S. Economic Surprise Index fell deeply negative in mid-2022 as data kept surprising hawkish forecasts, then climbed back to around its 90th historical percentile by early 2026 as releases repeatedly beat consensus.
